landmarks.name: Stari Most
landmarks.writeup: A 16th-century Ottoman bridge in Mostar, symbolizing reconciliation and the country's diverse cultural heritage.

wiki.extract: The Old Bridge, also known as the Mostar Bridge, is a rebuilt 16th-century Ottoman bridge in the city of Mostar in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It crosses the river Neretva and connects the two parts of the city, which is named after the bridge keepers who guarded the Old Bridge during the Ottoman era. Commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent in 1557 and designed by Mimar Hayruddin, a student and apprentice of the architect Mimar Sinan, the Old Bridge is an exemplary piece of Balkan Islamic architecture.

landmarks.name: Vrelo Bosne
landmarks.writeup: A natural park featuring the spring of the River Bosna, known for its scenic beauty and walking trails.

wiki.extract: Vrelo Bosne is a public park and a protected Nature Monument established around the source of the Bosna river, featuring the system of numerous springs at the foothills of Mount Igman, in the municipality of Ilidža, on the outskirts of Sarajevo, capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Vrelo Bosne is one of the country's popular natural landmarks and provides a quiet escape from city life.

landmarks.name: National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina
landmarks.writeup: Houses important archaeological, historical, and cultural artifacts representing the country's heritage.

wiki.extract: The Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, often referred to as Bosnian Army, was the military force of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was established by the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 following the outbreak of the Bosnian War.

cultural_events.name: Sarajevo Film Festival
cultural_events.writeup: The largest film festival in Southeast Europe, showcasing regional and international cinema.

wiki.extract: The Sarajevo Film Festival is an annual film festival held in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. The premier and largest film festival in Southeastern Europe, it is also one of the largest film festivals in Europe. It was founded in Sarajevo in 1995 during the siege of Sarajevo in the Bosnian War, and brings international and local celebrities to Sarajevo every year. It is held in August and showcases an extensive variety of feature and short films from around the world.

cultural_events.name: Mostar Summer Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An event celebrating local music, dance, and cultural traditions in Mostar.

wiki.extract: Mostar is a city and the administrative centre of Herzegovina-Neretva Canton of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the historical capital of Herzegovina.

food_writeup: Bosnian cuisine blends Ottoman, Mediterranean, and Central European influences, featuring dishes like nevapi (grilled minced meat), burek (filled pastry), and Bosanski lonac (meat and vegetable stew).
brief_history: Bosnia and Herzegovina has a complex history marked by Ottoman rule, Austro-Hungarian administration, and Yugoslav federation membership. It declared independence in 1992, followed by a devastating war until 1995, after which the Dayton Agreement established its current political structure.
current_conflicts: Bosnia and Herzegovina faces political tensions among its ethnic groups, particularly regarding governance and constitutional reforms, but no active armed conflict.

commentary.inflation_management: The currency board pegging the convertible mark to the euro makes Bosnia an importer of euro-area monetary conditions. Inflation was near zero or negative through the mid-2010s (-1.6% in 2016, the series low) as euro-area disinflation spilled over. The 2022 shock hit hard: 14%, the series high, on energy and food imports. Disinflation was quick — 1.7% by 2024 — with a projected 3.9% for 2025. The board precludes active monetary management; adjustment runs through wages and prices.
commentary.debt_management: Public debt is low by regional standards: 20.6% of GDP in 2006, a low of 18.2% in 2007, rising to 47.1% in 2014 after flood-related borrowing and IMF programs, then falling steadily to a projected 29.9% in 2025. COVID pushed it temporarily to 37.2% in 2020. GDP grew from $12.9bn in 2006 to a projected $33.0bn in 2025. The currency-board regime and IMF anchors have kept fiscal policy conservative; debt sustainability is not a binding constraint.

key_events.event: Currency board provided stability during the global financial crisis; growth slowed sharply but the peg held.
Devastating floods and IMF programs pushed debt to 47.1% of GDP, the series high.
Deflationary episode bottomed at -1.6% amid weak euro-area spillovers.
COVID-19: debt rose to 37.2% of GDP on the economic contraction.
Inflation spiked to 14% on imported energy and food prices.
EU candidate status (granted December 2022) anchored reform momentum.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Prospects depend more on politics than macroeconomics: low debt and a credible currency board are strengths, but fragmented governance and slow reform constrain EU accession progress. Inflation should stay near euro-area levels given the peg. The upside is EU integration unlocking investment; the downside is political fragmentation or a slowdown in the EU, Bosnia's main trade partner, transmitting directly through the currency board.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
